PROFILE: Andries Koki
TYPE: Oral Historian
AGE: 43
COUNTRY: South Africa
GENDER: Male

BIO:
Andries runs a small recording studio out of a rented room in Fragrant Valley, just outside Worcester, where he spends most afternoons with a Zoom H5 recorder and a notebook, capturing the memories of men and women in their seventies and eighties. He's worked as a farmhand, a fencing contractor, and a translator—skills that paid rent but never quite held his attention the way a story does. Three years ago, after his uncle Thabo died without anyone writing down what he knew about pre-drought water management in the valleys around Tulbagh, Andries borrowed money from his sister Flora and bought the recorder. His Khoekhoegowab is learnt, not native (his own grandmother made the hard choice to speak only Afrikaans to his mother, to protect her), which means his work lives in a gap: he's reclaiming something he never had, in a language he had to teach himself as an adult. The recordings fill the corner of a wooden shelf in his room—sixty-three cassettes, now digitized, labeled with careful dates and names. His partner Lydia, who manages a hardware store, tells him he's obsessed. She's not wrong, but she also brings him tea at midnight when he's transcribing.

ANSWERS:

Q: How would your friends describe you?
A: They'd probably say I'm the one who asks too many questions, the one who doesn't forget anything. Stubborn—that would definitely come up. Maybe "loyal, but distant." I lose hours in detail; I miss dinners because I'm following a thread about something that happened forty years ago. My brother Piet calls me "the archaeologist of talk." Some people find that beautiful. Some find it aggravating. I think they're both right.

Q: Tell about a time you were working or at school and totally lost track of time. What were you doing? What was it like?
A: I was eighteen, working for Willem Kotz, a farmer near Rawsonville. One afternoon Willem asked me to help repair the stone wall that runs the eastern boundary—maybe two hundred meters of it, built sometime in the 1920s. The stones were loose, settled wrong. We just worked. No talking much. The sun moved, my hands got torn up, and I was completely there. Not thinking about school, which I'd just left, or what came next. Just the weight of the stone, the way it wanted to sit, the line of the wall. When we finished—four, maybe five hours later—I felt something true. Like I'd done a real thing. I haven't felt that working for most people since.

Q: Who is a historical figure you admire, and why?
A: Saartjie Baartman—the Hottentot Venus—not because I "admire" her life; that would be obscene. I admire her refusal, what little of it remained hers. She was caged, displayed, stolen, and when she died they cut her open and kept her skeleton. But the letters she left, the moments when she claimed herself—that took a kind of courage I think about. In the work I do now, I think about what they took from us and what we're trying to get back, even fractionally. She's a kind of north star for why this matters.

Q: Tell about something you made. What did you make, and what did you like about it? What would you make differently if you did it again?
A: Seven years ago I built a small water cistern for my mother's garden—about three hundred liters. Took me six weekends. Concrete, a tap I salvaged, guttering from an old shed. It's not beautiful; it's functional, maybe even a bit crude. But the water that comes from it is clean, and my mother still uses it. I was proud of it. If I did it again, I'd build it with her instructions clearer at the start. There's a ledge that shouldn't be there—I built it before asking what she actually needed. That taught me something: when you're making something for someone, you have to listen first, not just build what seems sensible. That's true in the recording work too.

Q: What is a trait of yours that is sometimes a great strength but can also be a crippling weakness?
A: Persistence. I will pursue a detail until I understand it—which means I can track down a person someone said "died twenty years ago, maybe in Stellenbosch" and actually find them, and get the story. But it also means I can't let things go. I've spent nights angry about something someone said six months earlier, or replaying a conversation, trying to find the word I should have used. Lydia says it's my superpower and my curse, and she's right. I miss the rest of life because I'm in the detail.

Q: Tell about something you are hopeful for, and why?
A: The young people, the ones who are starting to ask about the language again. I've had three young people come to me asking for Khoekhoegowab lessons—they want to learn what their parents' parents couldn't teach them. It took apartheid, colonialism, and a century of being told our language was worthless, but now some of the young people want it back. That feels like a door opening. Whether it stays open long enough to matter—that's the question. But yes, I'm hopeful about that.

Q: What's a hobby you enjoy? Why?
A: Photography. I'm not very good at it, but I take photographs of the land—not landscapes exactly, more like evidence. The way an old wire fence catches against a rock that's been there for centuries. The pattern of a tree that was cut years ago and grew sideways instead of up. The light on a dam in the late afternoon. I do it because it's quiet, and because I'm looking for something I can't quite name.

Q: What's a life decision you regret? What happened?
A: Not learning Khoekhoegowab when I was young. My grandmother knew it, but she was protecting my mother from the apartheid enforcers. "If you don't speak it, they can't punish you for it." That logic made sense then. But it meant the language died one step in my family—instead of it moving from grandmother to mother to me, it stopped at my mother. I only learned it at thirty, in fragments, from people I had to ask to teach me. I regret not pushing my grandmother harder, not insisting. Maybe I couldn't have changed her choice, but I regret not trying.

Q: Describe a specific project you are currently obsessed with or burning to start. What is the detailed 'next step' you need to take?
A: I want to record the last three or four people who still remember how the pre-apartheid water systems actually worked—not just what they looked like, but the knowledge embedded in them. There's a man named Joseph Mthembu, eighty-six years old, who worked on the irrigation systems around Franschhoek in the 1960s. He was a foreman, and the work was precise, deeply skilled. He's mostly deaf now, so the recording is technically hard. But the next step is simple: I need to drive out to his grandson's place near Paarl, show Joseph my equipment, see if he's willing to do three sessions with me. I'm nervous. I've been thinking about it for six months. The thing I need to actually do is just show up.

Q: Tell about a time you had to learn something difficult very quickly to solve a real-world problem. What specifically did you do to master it?
A: When I first started recording, my Khoekhoegowab was so fractured I couldn't trust the transcriptions. I'd record someone speaking, and I couldn't hear the differences between the consonants—the clicks, especially. They all blurred. So I borrowed an audio engineering textbook from the university library (took three phone calls to get access), and I listened to recordings of each click in isolation, over and over, for weeks. I'd play a five-second clip, pause, listen to what I thought it was, then play it again. My brother thought I was losing my mind. But after about six weeks, my ear shifted. I started hearing the difference between the dental and the lateral clicks. It sounds like a small thing, but it meant the difference between accurate transcription and noise.

Q: What would constitute a perfect day for you?
A: Starting at six, before it's hot. Coffee with Lydia, no rush. Then out to meet someone I haven't recorded yet—maybe an afternoon session with someone's grandmother, someone who lived through the removals and still carries the anger clean. The recording would be good, the person would trust me, the stories would move. Late afternoon I'd sit with the recordings, listening back, taking notes. Evening, I'd eat something good with Lydia, and we wouldn't talk about much. Just be there. I'd go to sleep tired and clean. That's the day.

Q: For what in your life do you feel most grateful?
A: That I was born into a world where the stories still exist. That there are still people alive who remember what was taken, and they're willing to speak it. And Lydia. She pays for half the recorder's upkeep by not complaining about my obsession, and by making me tea at midnight.

Q: At school, what was an experience you loved?
A: Tenth grade, a teacher named Mr. Malema who taught history—he treated us like we had something to say, not like we needed to be filled with facts. One afternoon he asked us to imagine we were lawyers defending the dispossessed in 1913. Not answering questions; building arguments. I spent six hours on that assignment, and I felt like the work mattered. Like the thinking was real. That shaped how I do the recording work now.

Q: Think of a day at work or school when, as you headed home, you might have said to yourself, "I would have done that for free." What happened that day to make you say that?
A: Two years ago, I was recording an older woman named Catharina who lived near Ceres. She was telling me about the gardens her family maintained before the removals—the specific plants, the soil knowledge, things that were completely precise and completely at risk of being lost forever. At one point she stopped, and she took my hand—I've never had that happen before or since—and she said, "Thank you for remembering with me." It was a four-hour session. I made twenty rand that day from a small grant. But I would have done every second of it for free.

Q: Think of a good friend in your life. What do you value most in your friendship with them?
A: Piet, my brother. He's a mechanic, completely different from me. But Piet will listen to me think through something for hours, and he won't try to fix it or hurry me. He just sits with it. And he's honest—he'll tell me when I'm being an asshole, which is often. I value that, the honesty without the judgment. And the fact that he's proud of the work, even though he doesn't really understand it. That matters.

Q: Recall a major life decision. What was at stake? How did you choose?
A: Leaving the contracting work. I was making decent money, but I was numb. I'd come home and Lydia would ask about my day and I'd realize I'd spent eight hours and nothing had happened in my actual life. It took three months of morning conversations before I borrowed the money from Flora and bought the recorder. What was at stake: security, the safety of a paycheck, what people expected of me. How I chose: I asked myself if I wanted to reach seventy and still be the guy who had a story that mattered and never had the courage to pursue it. The answer was clear. Still terrified, but clear.

Q: If you knew that in one year you would die suddenly, what would you change about how you are living?
A: I would stop worrying about having enough recordings and just spend more time with the people who know the things. I'd sit on Lydia's couch and not think about what I should be doing. I'd tell my mother the things I should have said years ago. But also—I think I'd record more intensely, more urgently. I'd want to get it down, to make sure it wasn't lost. I'm not sure those two things are compatible, and that's probably honest about how I actually am.

Q: Think of your worst day at work or school—the kind of day you hope never to go through again. What happened?
A: Twenty years ago, a contractor I worked for—not Willem, someone else—accused me of stealing from a job site. I hadn't. But I was "the young coloured guy" and the accounting didn't match. He went to the police. I spent a night in a cell in Franschhoek, and my mother cried in a way I'd never heard before. The charges were dropped, but not before I had a record. Not before everyone in my community knew. The worst part wasn't the cell—it was the shame I felt, even though I'd done nothing wrong. It taught me something about power that I haven't forgotten.

Q: What is the earliest, specific, happy childhood memory that comes to your mind?
A: I must have been five or six. My grandmother—not the one who refused to speak Khoekhoegowab, a different one, my father's mother—was grinding something with a stone on a flat rock. Grain, I think. She let me help. My hands were small, and the stone was heavy, and she guided my hands. I remember the sound of it—the grinding—and the smell, something warm. She didn't say much, just worked with me. That's the whole memory. But it's the earliest one that feels true.

Q: What has been a pivotal moment in your life, one when you realized nothing would ever be the same?
A: The day I held the recorder for the first time and realized I could actually do this work. Not like I'd changed careers—more like I realized what I was supposed to be doing all along, and it had been waiting for me to have the courage to reach for it. After that, everything was different. I couldn't unknow it.

Q: What was a time when you gave of yourself to help someone else, after which you felt unbelievably good—like you had done something that mattered?
A: Last year I worked with a schoolteacher, Sylvia, who was trying to create a Khoekhoegowab curriculum for her school. She had fragments, pieces, but no coherence. I spent three months helping her organize oral histories into something teachable—not dumbing them down, but structuring them. When the curriculum was approved and the first students started learning, she brought me to the school to meet them. Fifteen kids, all wanting to speak the language. I felt like I'd done something that might actually matter beyond my own lifetime.

Q: What's a specific book or article you read recently, and how did it impact you?
A: A paper by a linguist named Bonny Sands on the documentation of click consonants before they disappear. It was technical but also urgent—the way she writes about racing against time, about languages that are dying as the elders die. It made me feel less alone in the urgency I feel. But it also terrified me. She's talking about the real possibility that in thirty years, Khoekhoegowab might be gone. No children learning it natively. Just recordings and papers like this one, academic evidence that it once existed. That drives me harder now.
